01 Why it matters

More than
just old clothes.

Uniforms are often retired because of branding, age or organisational requirements, even when portions of the fabric remain usable. Our project asks how those materials might be put to better use — through meaningful products, inclusive paid preparation work and creative activities for seniors.

206,000tonnes of textile & leather waste generated in Singapore, 2024
3%recycling rate for this national waste stream, 2024

National figures cover all textile and leather waste, not uniforms alone. Source: NEA 2024 waste statistics.

03 Collection

A better ending
begins with a return.

Begin with a small school-based collection pilot. With each school’s approval, accept clean, authorised retired uniforms, screen their condition, and record the results before considering expansion to SAF sites.

COLLECTION GUIDE / WHAT WE ACCEPT

Still useful. Still welcome.

Uniforms do not need to be perfect. What matters is that they are relatively clean, dry and have fabric we can safely reuse.

WE ACCEPT

Clean, used uniforms

Previously worn uniforms that are washed, dry and in reasonably good condition.

WE ACCEPT

Minor wear or damage

Small tears, loose stitching or fading are fine when enough usable fabric remains.

NOT SUITABLE

Soiled or heavily damaged

Please exclude wet, mouldy, contaminated or severely degraded uniforms.

✦ Proposed acceptance guidelines only. Collection must be authorised by the uniform owner; badges and identifying information will be securely handled before upcycling.

06 After preparation

One material.
Two new purposes.

After inspection, suitable materials can move through two complementary pathways. Select a pathway card to explore how the fabric could be used.

Pathway 01 / Commercial

Useful everyday products

Larger reusable panels could become hand-stitched pouches and other small-batch products for organisations or buyers.

A local upcycling maker would check fabric suitability, labour time, manufacturing cost and potential customer interest before increasing production.
Pathway 02 / Community

Make together, learn together

Clean, safe fabric offcuts could supply voluntary craft sessions for seniors at participating community centres.

Community partners would need suitable materials, facilitators, accessible session designs and participant feedback; the workshops are not intended as unpaid manufacturing labour.

A circular economy can create both products and participation.

BEYOND THE COLLECTION / FUTURE OPPORTUNITY

Made together.
Skills that stay.

Our vision does not end with selling upcycled products. By collaborating with corporate partners and training providers, Sew Much More could turn approved retired uniforms into hands-on workshops where people learn to repurpose fabric and design something useful.

Workshop participation fees and sponsored sessions could create an additional income stream, while participants develop practical skills in material reuse, basic sewing and thoughtful product design.

Photo: Pavel Danilyuk · Pexels

Potential team-building or sustainability sessions, with opportunities to support material collection and workshop costs.

Photo: August de Richelieu · Pexels
02 / EDUCATIONTraining providers

Co-develop accessible instruction on textile preparation, stitching, design choices and quality checks.

Photo: Los Muertos Crew · Pexels
03 / PEOPLEParticipants

Learn hands-on upcycling skills and take home an item they have designed and made themselves.

What might a beginner workshop look like? +

Example: a 2-hour drawstring pouch lab (proposed)

  1. Understand textile waste and safe material reuse
  2. Choose pre-cleaned, approved fabric and sketch a pouch design
  3. Practise measuring, cutting and basic stitching
  4. Assemble a drawstring pouch and learn finishing and care

Format, fees and learning outcomes would be agreed with future partners. Workshops are not currently open for booking.

09 Implementation

From a small pilot
to a lasting loop.

Our proposed rollout begins with a manageable school pilot, then expands only after safety, capacity and partner approvals are established. These are future steps, not confirmed collection arrangements.

01

Small pilot in schools

Partner with selected schools to trial collection of clean, retired uniforms. Agree on permissions, simple collection procedures and safe sorting, then measure how much fabric can be recovered.

02

Expand to SAF camps

Subject to SAF and MINDEF approval, extend the pilot to selected camps and SAFRA collection sites. Formalise secure handling, removal of identifiers, transport and preparation with appropriate partners.

03

Community engagement

Work with social enterprises on paid fabric preparation and community centres on elderly-friendly sewing workshops. Trial bags and pouches, involve volunteers and gather feedback on participation and product quality.

04

Full implementation

Scale up successful collection and upcycling routes across approved partners. Establish repeatable production, commercial sales and funding arrangements, while tracking material recovery and social impact.

A meaningful pilot must address secure identification removal, safe cleaning, fair paid work, product quality, buyer demand and management of unsuitable textiles.
10 Sew Much More.

Less discarded.
More possible.

Not every retired uniform will become a product. But a thoughtful collection and upcycling system could offer fabric a second use — and create opportunities for people along the way.

This experience visualises a proposal. All photographic scenes are illustrative, not documentation of completed group activities. Any eventual pilot would require real partners, permission and material testing.
